                         INTRODUCTION.


The Kegister of Burgesses and Guild-Brethren of the City of
Edinbm-gh is contained in a number of MS. vokimes, carefully
preserved     in   the   Town   Clerk's   fire-proof   safe   in    the   City

Chambers.
       After 30th May 1666 the entries of apprentices are contained

in the scroW volumes, along with those of burgesses                and guild-
brethren.      The roll of these is being issued separately.
       Of these volumes Nos. 1 to 8 have been used in compiling the
roll    which follows, beginning at 17th May 1487, and ending in
Vol. 8 at 31st December 1700.
    The very early entries are taken from the minutes or records
of the Town Council.    The scroll volumes, whose contents have
not been entered in the official volumes, or have been lost with

them, are very badly and hastily written, and in many cases the
names, christian and, more particularly, family, are very difficult
to decipher, the rather that no rule of spelling has been observed,

and the attempts at a phonetic rendering are bewildering.                 The
Celtic names are really dreadful.

                         being in ancient script, and also
       The   earhest entries,                                in

Latin abounding in contractions, offered obstacles which would,
it is   to be feared, have wrecked the undertaking, but for the help,

so graciously given, chieflyby Mr. John Jarvis, Session-Clerk
of the City Churches, by Mr. Henry M. Baton of H.M. Kegister

House, and by Miss Marguerite Wood, Keeper of the Burgh
Records, to all of whom I tender my very grateful thanks.

                                CHARLES B. BOOG WATSON.

                            Watson, born 1558.    Minister in St. Giles. Put in
 ward Jan. 15S6 for speaking boldly before the

to accept the King's story of the Gowiie conspiracy, he was banished for
a time in 1600.    He was one of the eight ministers summoned in 1606 to
appear before the King at Greenwich, and was warded with Dr. Vaughan,
Bishop of London. In 1607 he returned to his parish of Burntisland, whence
he was translated in 1615 to Markinch, where he died in 1619.

succession to the English crown. The nobles, gentlemen and household who
attended the banquet given on the 26th June were made burgesses and gild-
brethren gratis.

    7   March i66o.— Sir James Stanfield of New Milns, in East Lothian, and his
son Philip.    Sir James, a Yorkshire man by birth, is said to have been a
colonel on the Parliamentary side in the Civil War.       He came to Scotland,
after the battle of Dunbar, 1650, and having acquired certain lands on the south
bank of the Tyne, a mile east of Haddington, he set up a cloth manufactory,
named New Milns. Later he was knighted by Charles IL, and his cloth
industry was encouraged in 1681 by James, Duke of Albany and York, later
James VH.
     He also acquired property in Edinburgh, both in Blackfriars Wynd, and in
 what is now called World's End Close, where Sir Wm. Bruce of Baicaskie dis-
 poned part of his property to him, whence the close at one time bore the name
 of Stanfield's CI.   He also owned the ground in Leith whereon the glass work
 was built later.
     He was made a burgess and guild-brother of Edinburgh 7th March 1660,
being then secretary to General Major Thomas Morgan, gratis, and ;^5 voted
to him, for his good service done to the town.
     On 2 July 1679 Mr. Philip Stanfield, fiar of New Milne, was made burgess
and guild-brother of the burgh, gratis. He must have been Sir James' elder
and most unsatisfactory son, who was married, and lived in his fatlier's house.
    On the 28 November the body of Sir James was found among the ice in
a pool in the river.   It was secretly buried by his son, as that of a suicide.
    But the Lord Advocate, hearing of the case, gave orders for the exhumation
and examination of the corpse. This was carried out, and the surgeons per-
formed the autopsy, in the course of which they made an incision in the neck
of the deceased.    When Philip, at the request of the surgeons, lifted the head
of his dead father, to help in replacing the body in the coffin, the blood suddenly
showed on the linen swathing, and Philip, horror-struck, dropped his burden,
and fell back in a faint. In due course he was arrested, and tried before the
High Court of Justiciary in February 1688, and found guilty. Sir George
Mackenzie assisting the Lord Advocate in the prosecution. He was hanged at
the Market Cross, and his body was hanged in chains at the Gallow
                                                                       Lee, between
Edinburgh and Leith, and finally disappeared.
    The New Milns property was sold, on the winding up of the cloth company,
to the notorious Colonel Francis Charteris, who
                                                    changed its name to Amisfield,
                                              {^See "Twelve Scots Trials," by Wm.
after that of his family seat in Nithsdale.
Roughead, W.S., and "Sir Richard" in Sir Walter Scott's " Minstrelsy of the
Scottish Borders.")

            In the early admissions of burgesses                       payments of duty were sometimes "by
composition."   In some                              cases   spices    and wine, a banquet in fact, were
furnished, and accepted.
            Burgesses were often admitted by the provost, or a bailie, or the treasurer,
apart from the Dean of (iuild Court.
   When thus admitted by a bailie, it was by him as a bailie " et ea ratione."
This was corrected later.
            A master often is admitted burgess in order to be able to take an apprentice.
    The date, between brackets, in the entry of admission of a craftsman as
B. or G. by right of his apprenticehip, is that of his entering his master's
service.

            When a letter is given in brackets in a name, as in "Caldwell(s)," it indicates
that both forms (" Caldwell" and "Cald wells") are found.

            A good many entries appear twice, under different dates.
            If "gratis" be not mentioned, the burgess paid for his burgesship.

            Dates.   —    It   must be remembered that under the Old Style the year ended
24 March.

                         Jan.      \'-^oo {p.'^.')   succeeds 31   Dec. 1500, and should be written               i

    300- 1.
            The New Style was adopted ist Jan. 1600.
            There are very few addresses or residences given, e.g. "John Adamsone for-
nent the crose." 12 Jan. 1 570-1
   John Hamilton, "dwelland in Williamson's Close," 14 Jan. 1567-8.
    Residence. ^\Nhtn a man was made a burgess of Edinburgh it was necessary
for him to reside within the burgh.  Instances occur frequently of indwellers in
Leith, who, on being made burgesses, are required to remove and find residence
in Edinburgh, under the paine of tinsell (loss) of their freedome, eg. Francis
Aird and Rob. Dowglas, 27 Oct. 1669. Patrick Crightoun, mt. was forced to
leave tlie Canongate and reside in Edinburgh 17 March 1648.

    An applicant for burgesship could choose one qualification therefor, ratlier
                               —
than another probably preferring the cheaper.       Thus a man eligible as
'prenteis to an employer, or as guidson to a burgess, would choose the latter
qualification.
   Not infrequently a group of one trade entered as burgesses at one time a                                           —
bunch of tailors, hatmakers. or fieshers, while on special occasions, such as
banquets, or the honouring of a special family, as many as a hundred might be
admitted burgesses and gild-brethren, gratis. Such burgesses, however, as a
rule, enjoyed the privilege personally,                               without the   riglit   to transmit   it   to their
bairns.
    Moses Mosias, a Jew, was allowed to trade in the town, with a promise, for
his encouragement, that if he become a Christian, he shall be admitted

                                       ACT OF COUNCIL.
       Dec. 1615.
        15
                           —
                   "The same (day) the counsell haveing consideratioune and
respect to the guid service done to thame and thair predecessors be umquhyle
Johne Johnstoune, vvrytter, and umquhyle John Johnestoun, merchant, his sone.
Ordains David, Johne, Margaret and Kathreine Johnstoune's lavvfull bairns lo
the said umquhyle Johne Johnestoune, merchand, procrcat bctwixe him and
Jonet Wilkie, his spous, to be resavit burgesses and gildbrether of this burgh,
be rycht of the said umquhyle Johne Johnestoune, thair father, as iff the
said umquhyle Johne Johnestoune, merchand, be rycht of the said umquhyle
Johne Johnestoune, his father, quha wis bulges and gildbrother of this burgh
had bene admitted and ressaived burges and gildbrother of the samyne.
Dispensing with his admissione in that caice for the quhilk this present act sal
be ane sufficient warrand to the said deyne of gild and his successors in all
tyme cumniing."
   David was admitted B. and G. 29 Oct. 1634.

                INTRODUCTION.




In this volume    is   continued the Roll or Register

of   Burgesses and Guild-brethren of the        City   of

Edinburgh from 1st January 1701 to 31st December

1760.   Illustrative notes, glossary, etc., will be found


at the end of the volume.

       NOTES ON BURGESS ROLL, 1701-1760.

    The dates quoted in the Burgess Roll of the admission of a burgess or
guild l^rother by the Town Council are frequently incorrect, and sometimes
cannot be traced. A number of those admitted by the Council were never
admitted l)y the Dean of Guild and his court       their names are not on the
                                                   ;



register, and consequently do not appear in the MS. Index.      Occasionally a
burgess is admitted by the Guild Court by rin act of Council passed some
time after    Nor was admission by the Town Council promptly followed by
                           —
           I




that of the Guild Council  we find, for instance, Wm. Lumsdain was admitted
l)y the Town Council 5 Sept. 1744
                                       —
                                    and only six years later, 12 Oct. 1750, did
the Guild Council admit him.    John Russel, writer to the signet, admitted by
the Town Council 5 Aug. 1741, became 15. and G. only on 15 Sept. 1749, after
eight years' delay, while Dr. Robert Hay waited for nearly ten years, from
28 May 1740 to 10 Jan. 1750, ere he became a "freeman."
    But the apprentices were far more dilatory.
       Robert Thomson, skinner, entered      p.   18 July   171 1, burgess   18   Feb.
           1747-
       John Somervail, wright, entered p. 3 Mar. 1797, burgess 11 Feb. 1736.
       Robert Young, wright, entered p. 23 Oct. 1682, burgess 19 Sept. 1722.
       Robert Tod, wright, entered p. 18 July and 22 Aug. 1705, burgess
          7 Mar. 1750.

    Evidently there was no advantage to be gained by early admission.
    The same may be noticed in the case of guild brethren, entering sometimes
long after admission as burgesses.
    It is c|uite evident that despite all the care taken in entering apprentices,

burgesses and guild brethren, omissions have occurred.            We find men
admitted burgesses as apprentices who are not entered in the apprentice roll         ;


or others entered by right of a father burgess, whom we seek in vain in the
burgess roll.
    Occasionally the Council passed a second act admitting some one as B.
and G., apparently forgetting that this had been done already.
    Admission as a burgess and guild brother without payment of dues               —
           —
"gratis" was in many cases purely complimentary, and conferred no rights
or privileges, unless particularly specified.
    In some cases it was granted "for good service done," such as the ad-
mission of Wm. Blair, gratis, "for good service done at the late fire in the
head of the West Bow (79 Sept. 17 10)
    In at least one case the widow of a burgess and guild brother seems to
have conferred the right of admission on her second husband. See Thomas
Espline, 30 Aug. 1710.
   Note.   —
           The form of the entry in the Minutes of Town Council diflfers
       occasionally so far from that in the Burgess Roll as to make it worth
       while to note both. Where no "right of admission" is mentioned, the
       admission is by payment as exigible from an "unfreeman."

   The paucity of cutlers within the city may be gauged by the entry of
Robert Boog, 26 Apr. 1748, when there was "no quorum of their craft within
the city," and the Town Council had to assume the responsibility.
   Chairmasters seem to have been admitted invariably on payment of the
dues as unfreemen. They served no apprenticeship, and, curiously enough,
seem to have had no right by parentage or marriage.

                     — Act of Council in favour of the freemen burgesses.
      The following acts were exhibited, and appointed to be intimate yearly by
tuck of drum, against abuses committed by unfree persons             in the   land mercat
and elsewhere, viz.          :
                                 — Act of 8 May 1607         ;



                                          16 July 1647 ;
                                          17 Oct. 1656       ;



                                          14 Feb. 1688,
forbidding hawking at private houses except on the market day, viz. Wednesday,
between g a.m. and i p.m., between the Weigh-house and the Luckenbooths.
None allowed to sit down in front of the stands but must take stands for
themselves.  No retailers (hucksters) allowed, only makers of what they sell.
No one allowed to keep unsold goods within the town. The bailie of the
Butter Mercat empowered to put this into effect.

                     Benjamin Ramage, p. to Adam Watkins,
                                                       "
                                                               H.M. Printer and
 Stationer for Scotland, B.   In the privately printed   Reminiscences" (p. xxxv)
 of Charles Cowan of Logan House, ex-M.P., speaking of the paper mills at
 Valleyfield, Penicuick, he says, "they were occasionally possessed
                                                                    and wrought
 by the King's printer of the day. There is a tradition in the parish that a
 King's printer, named Watkins, about the middle of last {i.r. i8th) century met
 with a very appalling death.       He had been a very godless man, and one
 Sunday he had been walking with a friend towards Pennicuick House during
 the hours of divine service, when a storm of thunder and lightning suddenly
 set in  ;
          he blasphemously defied the power of the Almighty, and was immed-
 iately struck down dead.      It created a great sensation in the congregation,
 who were informed of the death by the officiating minister before the close of
 the service."

    2^ June 1712.— (George Bailie.)
                                           —
                                     The Maiden Hospital was in 1695 founded
by the craftsmen of Kdinburgh and Mary Erskine, relict of James Hair,
druggist, burgess of Kdinlnirgh, she being "the first who projected and
destinated funds for Maiden Hospitals in the City of Edinburgh."           She
accordingly bears the Title of the Founder of the Hospital, and it is provided
that two of the name of Erskine shall be for ever governours thereof, named in
the first instance by herself- these two being (probably as relatives; the
notorious Master James Erskin of (irange, Senator of the College of Justice,
who marooned his mad wife in St. Kilda, and Master David Erskine, advocate.
The governors, by grant from the Town Council, enjoyed the right of nominat-
ing one man annually for admission as a burgess gratis.

    22 Mar. 1717.       —
                     Act of Council, in view of abuses in persons, other than
burgesses, keepmg shops, etc., that in future any one wishing to be made a
burgess, and having right thereto, must enter within three years after their
minority, or marriage, or expiry of apprenticeship, otherwise they shall lose the
right, and also pay twenty pounds
                                    Scots for each year they shall so trade.
    Farther that no women, other than widows or daughters of burgesses, shall
be allowed to keep shops, and this in special view of the fact that so many
servants quit service and open shops, causing dearth of servants and unfair
competition.
   And farther, that no one be eligible for any office, which necessitates guild
brotherhood, unless he be already a guild brother.

    \b July 1718.— In consequence of a petition given in by the maltmen and
brewers of Leith against unfreemen who have taken up the trade of brewing
in Leilh, underselling the legitimate brewers, and encouraging smuggling and
hidden trade, the Town Council discharge all persons other than burgesses of
Edinburgh and incorporate maltsters of Leith to take up or carry on the trade
of brewing in Leith, under pain of one hundred merks Scots. A number of
unfree brewers in Leith entered burgesses of Edinburgh accordingly.

       17 Oct. 1722.
                       — Act   in   favour of Charles Dallas, for delivery of his burges
ticket, of which he had been deprived, and also fined, for printing and publishing
a paper called the Edinburgh News Letter, containing several scandalous
speeches and poems, without licence, contrary to an act of Council. He pleads
ignorance of the said act, blushes for and is ashamed of his action, and has
found caution to behave himself civilly and forbear the like practices in time
coming.
    25 Mar. 1724.
                       —
                    James Brownhill, wright, late burgess and guild brother, had
been convicted of being accessory to an attempt made on the house of Andrew
Wardrope, late Deacon convener, for the purpose of seizing a banner or ensign
belonging to the craftsmen of the city. Part of his punishment was the loss of
his freedom as burgess and guild brother.   He is now most penitent and craves
reinstatement, which is granted.
    (Builder of "James" Court, Lawnmarket.)

    I Sept.                                     —
             1725 (entered after 22 Sept.) The Lord Provost, Bailies, Council,
and Deacons of Crafts, considering the arrears due to the Dean of Guild's
accepting bills and other securities in payment of dues of burgess and gild
brother's tickets, whereby receivers of such tickets and their children enjoy the
benefits and privileges of the city without having paid therefor, ordain that no
one paying for his burgess ticket by bill or other security, shall receive said
ticket till the Dean of Gild be satisfied and the dues paid, and no clerk shall
extend or give out any such ticket without the Dean of Guild's warrant.

discharged to trade as ane unfreeman."

    1 June 1731.— The Council considering the act of Council of 24 Dec. 1703

limiting the import of gratis burgess tickets to a term of five years,
                                                                             and
considering that there is no distinction made in the tenor of gratis tickets that
are given to such as are servants to H.M. Commissioners to the General
Assembly, and to such like, from the honorary tickets that are given to noblemen
and gentlemen in compliment, do ordain that hereafter in all gratis tickets
which are not given in compliments to noblemen and gentlemen, that there
shall be an explicit reference to the said act of Council, limiting the term for
which the freedom is thereby intended, and appoints the gratis tickets granted
26   May to the Earl of Loudon's servants to be made out after that tenor.

withstanding his father's ommission would allow him to enter in right of his
grandfather and to authorise the Dean of Gild to admit him accordingly, more
especially as the petitioner by the mother's side is descended of a very ancient
race of burgesses and has also a right to enter by his wife as the petition bears.
Which haveing been read in Council the same was remitt to a committee of
    their number and they to report.     Accordingly this Day Baillie Robert Baillie
    from the said committee reported that they haveing considered the said
    petition, and altho' the petitioner's father neglected
                                                              or att least by his sudden
    death was prevented from entering in right of his wife yett as the petitioner
    himself has right to enter by his wi.^'e, lawfull daur. to Charles M'Hardie, mert.
    That therefor the Dean of Gild and his Council should be ordered to admitt
    the petitioner a burges and gild brother in right of his grandfather, by which
    no manner of loss is sustained by the city as the fees of entering in both cases
    are the same as the report under the hands of the Committee bears.             Which
    haveing been considered by the Magistrates and Councill they with the
    extra'ry deacons approved of the said report and ordered the Dean of Gild and
    his Councill to admitt and receave the petitioner to be burges and gild brother
    of this city in the right of John Jollie, mt., his grandfather, dispenseing with
    his father's ommission.   Whereanent ane extract of these presents shall be a
    warrant."

                     "Appointed the Dean of Gild and his Councill to admitt and

    dues in consideration of his ingenuity in contriving a loom for weaveing
    herron nets."

    18 June 1755.— "Mr. David Flint, old Dean of
                                                       Gild, represented he was
well informed that Richard Beckford,
                                         esquire. Member of Parliament for the
City of  Bristol, had been generously pleased to signify that he was to give two
hundred pounds Jamaica currency annually for the four ensuing years in order
to promote the exportation of linnen made in Scotland from the Port of Leith.
Therefore moved the Councill that they would be pleased as a mark of their
gratitude for this singular favour to the country and to the City of Edinburgh
in particular to order a burges ticket, for Mr.
                                                 Beckford, and to recommend to
the city's member when he goes next to Parliament to deliver it himself with
the Councill's best compliments.      Which having been considered        by the
Magistrates and Council), they appointed the Dean of Gild and his Councill to
admit and receive the said Richard Beckford a burges and gild brother of this
city, dispensing with the Dues for the good services done by him to the interest
thereof.   Whereanent these presents shall be a warrant."
    18 July 1755.— Philip Yorke, Lord Royston
                                                   (b. 30 Dec. 1723, d. 20 Jan.
1770), afterwards 2nd Earl of Harwick, and (1770) Lord High Chancellor, was
the eldest son of Philip, ist Earl of Hard wick, byMargaret   Cocks.
   The entry in the Burgess Roll reads -.— iZJuly 1755.—" The which Day the
Right Honble. George Drummond, Esq., Lord Provost [of] the City of
Edinburgh, James .Stuart, Robert Forrester, George Lind and John Lear-
month, baillies of the said city, James Grant, Dean of Gild, and the Gild
Council, did and hereby do invest with the freedom of this city Philip,
Lord Roystoun, in testimony of their grateful sense of the many eminent
services done to Great Britain by The Right Honble.
                                                      Philip, Earl of Hardwick,
Lord Chancellor, and his Lordship's particular attention to the improvement of
this part of the United Kingdom, conform to an act of the Town Council of this
date."
    (The said act is much more concise.)
    Among the "eminent services" were the Earl's presiding at the trial of
the Jacobite peers after Culloden, in which capacity he must hear
                                                                        large
responsibility for the cruelly vengeful verdicts pronounced and executed.   It
was due to him that the act was passed in 1748, for disarming the Highlands
and making the wearing of the kilt a criminal offence. The abolition of
"
 Hereditary Jurisdictions" in 1746 must, however, be put to his credit.
   Note.— 2 Feb. 1757.— Gilson, Mr. Cornforth, B. and G., gratis, "for the
eminent services done by him to this city by improving the taste of the
inhabitants in churcii music." He was appointed precentor of the new church
13 Mar. 1757, with /$ above the other precentors, teaching them and the
church music schools.
